cases.outcome: Egypt and Assyria survive diminished; Hittites, Mycenaean palaces and Ugarit fall
cases.mechanism: Trade-route breakdown, drought and raiding hit interdependent palace economies together.
cases.rhyme: Chokepoint and supply-chain attrition (Hormuz).
cases.note: Causes are debated; drought evidence comes from pollen and other proxy records.

cases.outcome: Augustan Principate prevails over senatorial factions
cases.mechanism: Surplus elites and soldiers loyal to generals rather than the state; the winner absorbed rivals into a new hierarchy.
cases.rhyme: Intra-elite conflict and divided government.

cases.case: Western Rome falls, Byzantium survives (376-476 CE)
cases.outcome: East survives; West falls
cases.mechanism: The West lost its North African tax base (439 CE); the East had defensible geography and secure revenues.
cases.rhyme: Geography and secure revenue as luck, not virtue.

cases.outcome: Tang survives, crippled; frontier governors keep fiscal power
cases.mechanism: Military governors captured tax collection permanently.
cases.rhyme: Fiscal fragmentation after a shock.

cases.outcome: Labour gains after the plague; manorial lords lose
cases.mechanism: Labour scarcity raised real wages despite wage caps.
cases.rhyme: Shocks that reprice scarce inputs (labour then; power and chips now).

cases.outcome: Qing coalition prevails; Ming falls
cases.mechanism: A silver-based tax system under monetary and climate stress; cuts to the courier service turned state workers (Li Zicheng among them) into rebels.
cases.rhyme: Fiscal rigidity meeting an external monetary shock.
cases.note: The 'silver crisis' explanation is contested among historians.

cases.outcome: Dutch prevail; Spain defaults repeatedly
cases.mechanism: Cheap, credible public borrowing beat costly short-term loans.
cases.rhyme: Borrowing costs as strategic capacity (10-year near 5%).

cases.outcome: Britain prevails; the old regime falls
cases.mechanism: Debt service crowded out the French state; Britain kept credible finance.
cases.rhyme: Debt service vs fiscal room.

cases.outcome: Japan prevails in 1895
cases.mechanism: Central tax and credit vs provincial fragmentation that starved logistics.
cases.rhyme: State capacity over hardware on paper.

cases.outcome: Early leavers (UK 1931, Sweden, Japan) recover sooner than the gold bloc
cases.mechanism: Abandoning a rigid monetary rule early freed domestic credit.
cases.rhyme: Policy rigidity in a downturn (Fed hiking into an oil shock).
cases.note: Well supported in economic history (e.g. Eichengreen and Sachs, 1985).

cases.outcome: Volcker Fed and non-OPEC producers win; price controls and leveraged borrowers lose
cases.mechanism: High prices cut oil intensity and drew new supply; tight money broke inflation at the cost of recession.
cases.rhyme: Oil shock plus a hiking Fed.

cases.outcome: China's reforms succeed; the USSR collapses
cases.mechanism: Oil-dependent budgets and frozen institutions vs dual-track reform.
cases.rhyme: Commodity-dependent states under sanctions (Russia, Iran).

cases.outcome: The imperial centre weakens while regional states (Bengal) stay productive
cases.mechanism: Political fragmentation without uniform economic collapse.
cases.rhyme: A weaker centre is not the same as economic failure.
cases.note: A 'false positive' for collapse theories; recent scholarship stresses regional vitality.

cases.outcome: Reform without fiscal independence; default (1875), foreign debt administration (1881)
cases.mechanism: Borrowing to modernise ended in creditors controlling part of state revenue.
cases.rhyme: Debt service limiting sovereignty.

cases.outcome: Institutions adapt; the state survives the Depression
cases.mechanism: Bank holiday, deposit insurance and new regulators changed the rules while the state could still act; wartime mobilisation finished the recovery.
cases.rhyme: Rule changes while capacity remains.
cases.note: The New Deal alone did not produce the full recovery.

cases.outcome: Republic falls; Hitler appointed chancellor in January 1933 without a Nazi majority (37.3% in July 1932)
cases.mechanism: Elite bargaining with a radical movement during economic catastrophe and rule by emergency decree.
cases.rhyme: Elite decisions, not only votes, decide regime outcomes.

cases.outcome: Relative decline without domestic collapse
cases.mechanism: Accepting a smaller role (Suez 1956 exposed the constraint) preserved the state.
cases.rhyme: Losing international power is not losing the capacity to govern.
cases.note: Suez was not the sole cause of British decline.

cases.outcome: Southern interior kingdoms (Tikal, Copan) collapse; northern Yucatan and coastal polities endure
cases.mechanism: Repeated drought on a deforested, rain-fed interior met kingships whose legitimacy rested on monuments; trade and people shifted to coastal routes.
cases.rhyme: Water and energy limits under prestige spending; activity moving to better-supplied corridors.
cases.note: Drought evidence comes from cave and lake cores; how much drought explains the collapse is debated.

cases.outcome: Mongol-Yuan conquest; Jin and Southern Song fall
cases.mechanism: The Southern Song had world-leading output but financed defence by printing paper money (huizi) into inflation while facing a better-organized military-commercial rival.
cases.rhyme: Rich economy, weak fiscal capacity for defence; monetary financing of deficits.

cases.outcome: Songhai (Gao) displaces the Malian centre
cases.mechanism: An empire built on taxing trans-Saharan gold and salt lost revenue as trade routes and rivals shifted.
cases.rhyme: Toll-based revenue exposed when traffic finds another route (Hormuz bypasses, regional payment rails).
cases.note: The document credits Portuguese coastal shipping; Portuguese voyages reached the West African coast mainly from the mid-1400s, after Mali's decline had begun, so their role is debated.

cases.case: Black Death and the Mamluk crisis (1347-1420)
cases.outcome: Venice and western European wage earners recover; the Mamluk agrarian tax base declines
cases.mechanism: Plague killed the labour that maintained Egypt's irrigation canals; a rigid tax-farming elite could not adapt, while labour scarcity raised western wages.
cases.rhyme: Deferred maintenance of physical systems (grid, water, ports) as the unpriced risk.

cases.outcome: Ottoman and Safavid states rise; Timurid princedoms and Mamluk cavalry lose
cases.mechanism: States that standardized artillery, firearms and their logistics overturned cavalry-based rivals.
cases.rhyme: A military-technology shift (drones, cyber, AI) rewarding whoever organizes the logistics first.

cases.case: Inca civil war and Spanish conquest (1525-1572)
cases.outcome: Spanish-indigenous coalition prevails; the Cuzco centre falls
cases.mechanism: Smallpox reached the Andes before the Spanish did, killing the ruler and his heir and setting off a succession war that the invaders' indigenous allies exploited.
cases.rhyme: An external shock to the top of a centralized system, then rivals exploit the split.
cases.note: The document says quipu records 'prove' this; quipus are largely undeciphered, and the evidence comes from Spanish and indigenous colonial-era accounts.

cases.outcome: The shogunate avoids deforestation and silver-drain crises without expansion
cases.mechanism: Forest rationing and replanting, restricted bullion export and domestic rice and copper money stabilized a closed economy.
cases.rhyme: Managed steady-state adaptation as an alternative to growth (efficiency, grid and resource rationing).
cases.note: Stability came with tight social control and closed borders, costs the document does not weigh.

cases.outcome: The Angkor core declines gradually; power and trade move to southern and maritime centres
cases.mechanism: A hydraulic network of roughly 1,000 square kilometres strained under alternating long droughts and extreme monsoons; land use in the core was already falling in the early 1300s, long before the traditional 1431 date.
cases.rhyme: Activity drifting away from aging central infrastructure (grid, water, ports) rather than a single collapse date.
cases.note: Sediment and pollen evidence moves the story from sudden conquest to long transition; figures are the document's, not re-verified here.

cases.outcome: Tenochtitlan falls to a Spanish-indigenous coalition; Nahua communities and institutions persist locally
cases.mechanism: A tribute empire with many resentful subject city-states; smallpox struck before the 80-day siege, and rivals of the Mexica supplied most of the besieging force.
cases.rhyme: Alliances that rest on extraction invite defection when a shock arrives.
cases.note: The Florentine Codex preserves Nahuatl testimony on the epidemic; Spanish accounts overstate European agency.

cases.outcome: After Mongke's death (1259) the empire splits into four khanates with different survival paths
cases.mechanism: Extraordinary mobility and elite integration, but no durable succession rule across a continent; khanates that stayed closer to steppe institutions lasted longer than the sedentary Yuan and Ilkhanate.
cases.rhyme: Fragmentation is not disappearance: successor systems with different survival odds.

learning.rules:
lens direction   a lens is flagged when it has pushed the wrong way on at least 10 resolved questions AND a
                   one-sided binomial test against 50% gives p < 0.10
  calibration      a probability bin is flagged when it holds at least 10 resolved forecasts and the observed
                   frequency lies outside the bin's 90% Wilson interval
  basis            a basis (market-anchored, base rate, judgment prior, judgment-heavy) is flagged when its mean
                   Brier is worse than its own base rates' mean Brier on at least 10 resolved questions

guide.title: User guide

start.text: Each question has a yes/no outcome, a date and a written resolution rule. The number shown is the model's chance that it resolves Yes. Resolved questions show Yes or No and are scored.

The range is the model's own doubt: lens scores scaled by half and by one and a half, and the base rate moved up and down in log-odds (twice as far when the base rate is a judgment prior). A rival inside that range is inside the model's doubt; it is not a confidence interval.
How often this kind of event happened in its reference class, before any evidence about now. Each question cites its reference class.
A prediction-market or option-implied price for the same or a closely related event, blended in by contract quality (see How the model works). 'Proxy' means the contract differs from the question.
What drives the number: market-anchored, base rate, judgment prior (reference class cites no data), judgment-heavy (lenses moved it more than one log-odds unit), or derived from other questions.
Points moved since the previous publication. The ledger scores only the first forecast, so later moves never improve the score.
Green: the last audit found no flaws (tests, ledger chain, simulation, nesting, data freshness, published data, overdue questions). Amber: a flaw; the next run reviews and republishes.

tabs.text: Every question in one place; click a question for its full card: what moved it from the base rate, reasoning, markets, rivals, history, data signals, what to watch, challenges and its ledger record.
How questions move together in the joint simulation. These follow from the typed factor loadings and the shared escalation root (judgment), not measured data.

This week and this month in history (dated rhymes, weight 0), the climate now, what calendar, climate and pattern evidence says for each testable question with its walk-forward skill and weight, tripwires, and the long-range watch list.
Each linked contract, its read time, quality gate and how much weight it gets.
Joint outcomes from the simulation (for example muddle-through, deal and disinflation), with how much they depend on the assumed correlations.
Every claim from rival models and documents, the verdict, the evidence and what changed in the model.
Scores of resolved questions against base rates and rivals; the hash-chained ledger of first forecasts.

how_it_works.text: Each forecast starts from a base rate in log-odds and adds evidence from five lenses: game theory, empire cycles, energy, capital and leaders. Scores are written into questions.py with their reasons; nothing is fitted to outcomes.
Questions that depend on a major US-Iran re-escalation share one root probability (R0) with a frozen rule; each question sees escalation only inside its own window (constant hazard).

Pooled with the model in log-odds by contract quality: exact and liquid 0.5, exact but thin 0.35, same test 0.35, proxy 0.2, option-implied 0.2, failing the quote-quality gate 0.1. A question broader than its contract cannot sit below the contract price unless it states an edge.

Calendar ('this time of year'), climate and pattern evidence is tested walk-forward against the base rate since 2000. It gets weight 0.2 only if its 90% interval of skill is above zero and it holds in a robustness grid; otherwise 0. Dated rhymes and cases always get 0.
A floor of 3% a year, scaled by the square root of the horizon, keeps room for the unknown.
200,000 correlated draws reproduce every forecast (error under 0.005) and give scenarios and pairwise links; a fat-tailed version is shown as a sensitivity.

The ledger records the first forecast for each question with a hash chain; resolution uses the question's own rule and named sources. About 109 resolved questions are needed before a 0.05 Brier gap means skill.

A daily review refreshes FRED, the Federal Register and Polymarket through the browser, checks the news, resolves questions and publishes when something changed. An audit runs every 3 hours and pushes a review early if it finds a flaw.

glossary.text: Mean squared error of probability forecasts against 0/1 outcomes; lower is better; 0.25 is a coin flip at 50%.
log(p / (1 - p)); evidence adds on this scale.
Each past month is predicted using only data available before it, then scored; nothing from the future leaks in.
1 - Brier(method) / Brier(base rate). Positive means the method beat the base rate.
A threshold on a published series that a document says would change the regime; the threshold is the document's choice.
A base rate whose reference class cites no number or dataset; its range is twice as wide.

playbook.intro: This section sums up three forecasts of how American society may adapt over the next decade, and what five groups might do about it: political leaders, business owners, professionals, skilled workers, and people in insecure work. These are the authors' views, not this model's forecasts, and not financial or personal advice. Each group's strategy is linked to the live questions it depends on, with the model's current probability.
playbook.outlooks: How the authors see 2035 (their judgment, not data): slow relative decline is the most likely path, at a little over 4 in 10. Genuine renewal gets about 1 in 5. A technology-driven leap and a severe hard reset share the rest, and this is where the authors disagree most. Each document's exact split is in History; where the documents overreach is under Arguments.
playbook.thesis: The United States is most likely to remain a major power that slowly loses ground to others, neither collapsing nor surging ahead. What tips it one way or the other is not how much money or technology it has, but whether it can turn them into things that work (power lines built, factories supplied, services delivered) and whether the gains are shared widely enough that people keep trusting their institutions.

tiers.exposure: Institutional: formal authority without operational capacity.
tiers.move_c: Reform before fiscal coercion forces it: broaden the tax base, remove privileges that undermine fairness, protect the agencies that deliver infrastructure, energy and emergency services, and keep transparent paths for elite competition.
tiers.move_g: Managed retrenchment: shed peripheral commitments while ring-fencing domestic solvency and reserve-currency credibility.
tiers.hedge_c: Keep professional administration, succession rules and state and local government working through a political crisis.
tiers.hedge_g: Standing liquidity backstops for municipal pension funds and regulated utilities before local rate revolts reach Treasury auctions.
tiers.trap: Protecting privileged exemptions while cutting the systems that make government work (Ming courier cuts, 1629; the Ancien Regime; Weimar austerity).
tiers.note: Both documents agree. The Ming courier cut as a cause of the dynasty's fall is contested (one factor among many). 'Byzantium survived by abandoning provinces' (Gemini) describes losses to conquest as a choice.
tiers.move_global: Shed open-ended peripheral military and financial guarantees; move budgets from administrative overhead to grid, water and transport maintenance.
tiers.hedge_global: Pre-authorized liquidity facilities for municipalities and utilities; drop rigid exchange-rate or austerity rules before deflation hollows the tax base.

tiers.exposure: Liquidity and confiscation: assets whose value depends on cheap financing, cheap energy or state support.
tiers.move_c: Own productive flexibility: businesses that earn under more than one scenario (generation and grid equipment, maintenance parts, domestic processing, efficiency, logistics and repair, infrastructure security).
tiers.move_g: Move from duration-sensitive, debt-dependent growth into physical bottlenecks (on-site power, grid hardware, refined fuels, mineral processing) plus short-duration government bills.
tiers.hedge_c: Manageable leverage, enough liquidity to survive delays and credit stress, no single supplier, financing source, customer or jurisdiction.
tiers.hedge_g: Custody across jurisdictions; avoid single-tenant vehicles that depend on continuous refinancing.
tiers.trap: Treating political importance, or a sovereign or quasi-sovereign guarantee, as economic resilience (Habsburg Spain's lenders; Ottoman bondholders after 1875).
tiers.note: That long-dated nominal bonds lost real value in 1973-1981 is well documented. Gemini's figure of a 20% fall in Dutch foreign trade is unverified here. These are the documents' general strategies, not investment advice; what they depend on in the model is the path of yields, the Fed and the AI-capex trade.
tiers.move_global: Rotate out of long-duration nominal debt and speculative software multiples into distributed power, grid hardware, water infrastructure, refined fuels and mineral processing.
tiers.hedge_global: Custody across neutral regional hubs plus short-duration bills; avoid single-tenant vehicles that need continuous rollover or subsidies.

tiers.exposure: Occupational: more credentialed candidates than institutional seats (elite overproduction), plus automation.
tiers.move_c: Move from institutional status to operational capability: electrical and industrial systems, infrastructure security, health care, automation and applied AI, logistics and compliance.
tiers.move_g: Leave compliance and middle-management layers for hands-on engineering, grid deployment and operations.
tiers.hedge_c: Portable skills: licences, portfolios, apprenticeships, cross-sector experience.
tiers.hedge_g: Portable equity and multi-client work instead of one salary.
tiers.trap: Defending credentials inside shrinking institutions (late Qing examination system, abolished 1905).
tiers.note: Meiji samurai redeployment and the 1905 exam abolition are standard history. The model has no data series on credential demand or AI displacement, so nothing here is tested.
tiers.move_global: Leave administrative and compliance layers for applied engineering, grid deployment, industrial logistics and clinical operations.
tiers.hedge_global: Portable certifications, equity in cash-flowing regional firms, cross-border remote capability.

tiers.exposure: Purchasing power, job stability, credit access and local infrastructure reliability.
tiers.move_c: Scarce practical skills that cannot easily be moved or postponed: electricians and grid technicians, mechanics, machining, health care, agriculture, water and utilities, transport.
tiers.move_g: Non-automatable trades plus fixed-rate housing; avoid variable-rate consumer debt.
tiers.hedge_c: Relationships beyond one employer: cooperative purchasing, credit unions, savings reserves, local repair networks, tools.
tiers.hedge_g: Local food and energy networks, credit unions, trade guilds.
tiers.trap: Depending on one employer or industry, or on nominal savings and unhedged debt through inflation (Weimar 1923; 1970s savers).
tiers.note: Post-1348 labour scarcity did raise real wages despite wage caps; Gemini's 'doubled by 1380' is stronger than most series show for that window (the large gains accumulate over the following century; not re-verified here).
tiers.move_global: Non-automatable trades (grid maintenance, mechanics, machining, health care, food production); fixed-rate housing; no variable-rate consumer debt.
tiers.hedge_global: Mutual-aid networks, credit unions, direct ties to local food and energy producers; household backup power and water storage.

tiers.exposure: Immediate access to resources; least ability to absorb a long disruption, but low fixed costs give flexibility.
tiers.move_c: Low fixed costs and several income sources: repair and resale, small logistics, food, contract and care work, local maintenance.
tiers.move_g: Low overhead and agile service, repair and resale in parallel markets that thrive when formal supply chains slow.
tiers.hedge_c: Mobility: keep documents, qualifications, transport and contacts so a move for work is possible.
tiers.hedge_g: Skill stacking and early moves toward regions with growing production and cheap water and energy.
tiers.trap: Depending entirely on one subsidy, patron or unstable institution, or on predatory debt (Rome after 439; Ottoman dependents after 1875).
tiers.note: The Soviet shuttle trade and Bengal's rise under Mughal fragmentation are standard history; informal markets in those cases also carried legal and safety risks the documents do not mention.
tiers.move_global: Minimal fixed overhead; repair, resale and local services; tool-based skills with no credential barrier.
tiers.hedge_global: Move early from high-cost, water-stressed cities toward regions with growing production and affordable land.

playbook.global_note: The model's 25-year global version tells the same story worldwide: the world splits into regional blocs, resource-rich regions gain leverage, and older, indebted economies retrench.

playbook.stage_note: ChatGPT's closing measure: resilience is the speed at which displaced resources, people, capital and institutions enter new productive arrangements before the old ones become unrecoverable, i.e. the gap between nominal resources and usable capacity. The model tracks that gap through the interconnection queue, transformer prices, state and local distress and productivity (History tab).
